issues.legal_issue: A permanent lease of endowed property granted by a shebait may be treated as valid beyond the grantor’s lifetime when the circumstances and long history of the transaction support a presumption that it was made for legal necessity.
material_facts: The properties were associated with a religious endowment, and shebaits granted permanent leases in 1869.

The grantors’ deeds recited that the endowment’s income was inadequate for its religious services and that the leased properties needed repairs or had become dilapidated; the arrangements secured rental income for the endowment, and one also provided cash for the deity.
The deeds and other circumstances indicated that the grantors were devoted to the endowment and were not seeking personal advantage.
By the time the leases were challenged, the original parties and other persons able to testify about the transactions had died.
Successive shebaits, guardians, and mortgagees recognized or did not challenge the leases’ permanent character for more than half a century.
issues.conclusion: The Court upheld the leases as made for legal necessity and binding on the deity, entitling the lessees to compensation for their permanent tenancy interests; the appeal challenging the leases was dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: Where the original parties and relevant witnesses to an old transaction are unavailable, recitals of its principal circumstances assume greater importance and should not be lightly rejected (Banga Chandra Dhar Biswas v. Jagat Kishore Chowdhuri, 43 I.A. 249). When a shebait’s permanent lease is challenged long after its grant and the circumstances cannot be fully ascertained, the Court should presume that it was made for necessity and is valid beyond the grantor’s lifetime (Bawa Magniram Sitaram v. Kasturbhai Manibhai, 41 I.A. 54). The recitals, the endowment-related purpose, and the long period without challenge supported that presumption here.

predicates.permanent_lease_challenged_in_endowment_: A party to a proceeding concerning a religious endowment challenged a permanent lease of endowed property.
predicates.original_parties_and_relevant_witnesses_: The original parties to the lease and other people able to give relevant evidence were no longer available to testify.
predicates.recitals_support_endowment_necessity: The lease documents recited circumstances indicating that the arrangement was needed or beneficial for the endowment and its religious services.
predicates.lease_unquestioned_for_long_period: Successive persons responsible for or interested in the endowment left the permanent character of the lease unchallenged for a long period.

issues.definition: When a permanent lease of endowed property is challenged in an endowment proceeding, the original participants and relevant witnesses are unavailable, the recitals support necessity for the endowment, and the lease went unquestioned for a long period, the lease is upheld as binding on the endowment.

issues.legal_issue: An appellate court generally should not interfere with concurrent findings of fact when a party has failed to prove the factual basis for its claim.
material_facts: The appellants claimed that money remained due under a usufructuary mortgage and sought compensation on that basis.
The Tribunal and the High Court both found that the appellants had failed to prove by proper evidence that any mortgage debt remained unpaid.
The Court considered the appellants’ arguments and found no reason to depart from the rule against interfering with concurrent findings on a pure question of fact.
issues.conclusion: The Court declined to interfere with the concurrent finding that the appellants had not proved an outstanding mortgage debt and dismissed the appeal.
issues.legal_principle: The Court has repeatedly held that it will not generally interfere with concurrent findings on a pure question of fact. The judgment identifies no particular earlier case for this principle.

predicates.civil_appeal_from_concurrent_factual_fin: A party brought a civil appeal against factual findings reached concurrently by the lower tribunal and court.
predicates.claimant_failed_to_prove_outstanding_mor: A claimant failed to provide proper evidence that money remained due under a mortgage.

issues.definition: When a civil appeal challenges concurrent factual findings and the claimant failed to prove an outstanding mortgage debt, the appellate court does not interfere with the concurrent factual finding.
